title: Checkpoint: Memory
objective: After this level you can explain how memories are stored, strengthened and rebuilt, and why they can mislead.
summary: Memory has three jobs: encoding, storage and retrieval. The chapter's studies each caught one going wrong, from the penny nobody encoded to memories rebuilt with details that never happened.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: every memory slip is a failure at one of three steps.
cards.body: Memory is a set of processes that encode, store and retrieve information: getting it in, keeping it, and getting it back out. Each study in this chapter caught one of those jobs going wrong.

cards.headline: Encoding: you can't lose what you never stored
cards.body: Could you pick out a real US penny from a set of similar drawings? In a 1979 study by Raymond Nickerson and Marilyn Adams, most Americans couldn't, despite a lifetime of handling pennies. They had encoded only enough detail to tell a penny from other coins. Distraction while studying does the same thing: information that never gets encoded can't be remembered later.

items.label: Getting it in
points: Working memory holds only about 4 chunks
Chunking packs more into each slot

items.label: Keeping it
points: Forgetting is steep at first, then levels out
Practice testing and spacing make memories last

items.label: Getting it back
points: Cues work best when they match the memory
Recall rebuilds, so misinformation can slip in

cards.headline: Not a video recording
cards.body: Memory, even for vivid events, isn't like a video. Its parts are stored in different places and put back together when you remember, and each step is a chance for error. That's why Ronald Cotton's case matters: a witness's honest certainty couldn't show that her memory was right.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How memories are encoded, stored and retrieved, and where each step can fail.
Why practice tests and spaced study beat rereading and cramming.
How recall rebuilds memories, letting suggestion add details that never happened.
Why a confident eyewitness can be wrong, and how fairer lineups help.

questions.prompt: Memory recap: what are memory's three basic jobs?

options.label: Sensory, short-term and long-term
options.rationale: Those are the stages of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, not the jobs.

options.label: Rehearsal, chunking and spacing
options.rationale: Those are strategies that help memory, not its jobs.

options.label: Seeing, hearing and feeling
options.rationale: Those are senses; memory's jobs come after sensing.

questions.explanation: Memory is the set of processes that encode, store and retrieve information.

questions.prompt: Memory recap: how does the 1979 penny study show encoding failure?

options.label: People never stored the penny's details in the first place
People stored the details but forgot them within minutes
options.rationale: The problem came before storage: the details never got in.

options.label: Leading questions changed their memory of pennies
options.rationale: No one was misled in this study; the details were simply never encoded.

options.label: The test room didn't match where they had seen pennies
options.rationale: That would be a context problem at retrieval, not encoding failure.

questions.explanation: People encoded only enough to tell a penny from other coins, so the details were never in memory to recall.

questions.prompt: Memory recap, from Level 32: what is working memory's capacity by current estimates?

options.label: Unlimited
options.rationale: Unlimited capacity is believed to belong to long-term memory.

options.label: About 15 to 30 seconds
options.rationale: That's how long short-term memory lasts, not how much it holds.

options.label: Exactly 7 items
options.rationale: Miller's "seven, plus or minus two" has been revised downward.

questions.explanation: Contemporary research, led by Nelson Cowan and others, puts working memory's capacity at about 4 chunks.

questions.prompt: Memory recap, from Level 36: in the 2006 study, what beat restudying on tests two days or a week later?

options.label: Taking recall tests on the material
Highlighting the key sentences
options.rationale: Highlighting was rated low utility in the 2013 review.

options.label: Rereading the passage faster
options.rationale: Rereading is restudying, which lost on delayed tests.

options.label: Studying in a louder room
options.rationale: Nothing in the study involved noise.

questions.explanation: Students who took recall tests remembered substantially more after days or a week than those who restudied.

questions.prompt: Memory recap, from Level 39: when is an eyewitness's confidence most informative?

options.label: When the witness is certain at trial
options.rationale: Certainty can grow after feedback, as in Ronald Cotton's case.

options.label: When the detective confirms the choice
When it's recorded at once after a fair, double-blind lineup
When the witness has seen the suspect on the news
options.rationale: Extra exposure after the event is a source of misinformation.

questions.explanation: Under clean conditions, a first confidence statement recorded right away is informative; certainty reached later can be inflated.
